The Story of Bira the Brahmin Woman

I bow to Lord Jina, who destroys all faults and bestows happiness, and I write the story of Bira the Brahmin woman, who condemned and confessed her own evil deeds.

This story is from the time when Duryodhan was king of Ayodhya. He was a very just and wise king. His queen was Shridevi, who was very beautiful and a true pativrata (devoted wife).

In that city lived a Brahmin named Sarvopadhyay. His wife's name was Bira. Her conduct was not good. She was intoxicated with the pride of youth. A student named Agnibhuti used to study at the upadhyay's house. Bira had an illicit relationship with him. The Brahmin woman loved him greatly. But the upadhyay was a thorn in the side of their happiness. Therefore, they could not enjoy their pleasure to their heart's content. This troubled the Brahmin woman greatly.

So one day, seizing an opportunity, the Brahmin woman killed her husband. Disguising herself to carry his body to the cremation ground, she left the house in the dark of night. Just as she was about to throw the upadhyay's body into the cremation ground, a Vyantar goddess, angry at such a wicked deed, pressed an umbrella onto her head and said, "When morning comes, you must go from house to house throughout the city, revealing your wicked deed to all the women, and confessing your guilt. Only then will this umbrella lift from your head."

According to the goddess's command, the Brahmin woman did exactly that. Only then was she freed, and the umbrella could be removed from her head. Through this self-condemnation, the Brahmin woman's sinful karma was greatly lightened. She was purified.

In the same way, other worthy souls should confess their evil deeds daily before their gurus. Through this, their sin will not increase, and they can keep their souls pure. Just as a person suffering from a thorn in the body cannot be happy until the thorn is removed, so too those who seek the soul's welfare, following the principles of Jain dharma and taking refuge in the passionless monks, remove the thorn of sinful karma through confession of their deeds. They then attain the imperishable wealth of the soul.

This story teaches that confession of sins is a powerful means of purification. Bira, though she had committed the terrible sin of murdering her husband, through sincere confession and self-condemnation, was able to purify her soul. The wise should never hesitate to confess their sins and seek guidance on the path of righteousness.
